title: Check and normalize a probability density
description: A continuous PDF must be nonnegative and have total area 1. Find the constant by integrating across its support.
recognize: A function f(x) with an unknown multiplier c is proposed as a density.
A question asks whether a function is a valid PDF: both sign and total area matter.

recipe.title: Identify the support
recipe.body: The support is the interval where the density can be nonzero. Use it as the integration limits.

recipe.title: Check the sign
recipe.body: Show that every factor is nonnegative on the support. A total area of 1 alone is insufficient.

recipe.title: Set total area to 1
recipe.body: Pull a constant outside the integral. Find an antiderivative, evaluate upper minus lower, and solve for c.
recipe.formula: 1=∫ f(x) dx=c∫ h(x) dx; c=1/∫ h(x) dx

recipe.title: Check the result
recipe.body: Substitute c back and verify sign and total area.

pitfalls: A density height can exceed 1. Only its total area must equal 1.
Use upper-limit evaluation minus lower-limit evaluation.

title: Find continuous probability as area
description: Integrate the density only over the requested interval, clipped to the support. A single point has zero area.
recognize: A PDF is given and the question asks P(a < X ≤ b).
A point probability P(X=x) for a continuous variable is always zero.

recipe.title: Write the event as an interval
recipe.body: Translate words such as between, more than, and within into inequalities.

recipe.title: Intersect with support
recipe.body: Values outside the support contribute no probability. Split at changes in the PDF if needed.

recipe.title: Integrate the density
recipe.body: Find area using an antiderivative H.

recipe.title: Check the size
recipe.body: The result must lie between 0 and 1. Endpoints do not change a continuous probability.

pitfalls: f(x) is density, not P(X=x).
Do not integrate x f(x) unless the question asks for expected value.

title: Build and use a continuous CDF
description: A CDF accumulates probability from the far left. Integrate a PDF to get a CDF; differentiate a smooth CDF to recover a PDF.
recognize: F(x)=P(X≤x) is supplied or requested.
Find an interval probability by subtracting two accumulated probabilities.
A median or percentile requires solving F(x)=target probability.

recipe.title: Include outer pieces
recipe.body: Before the support the CDF is 0; after it the CDF is 1.
recipe.formula: F(x)=0 below support; F(x)=1 above support

recipe.title: Accumulate area inside
recipe.body: Integrate from the lower support endpoint to x; use a dummy variable t.

recipe.title: Use the correct direction
recipe.body: Integrate f to get F. Differentiate F to get f where smooth.

recipe.title: Answer the event
recipe.body: Subtract CDF values for intervals or set F(m)=0.5 for a median.

pitfalls: A CDF must be defined for every real x.
For continuous variables, changing < to ≤ does not add probability.

title: Use lengths for a continuous uniform model
description: Equal-length intervals have equal probability. Divide favorable length by total eligible length, including conditioning if given.
recognize: Equally likely anywhere in a fixed interval signals Uniform(a,b).
A uniform arrival that has not occurred yet restricts the remaining interval.

recipe.title: Identify the full interval
recipe.body: Express the endpoints in matching units.

recipe.title: Restrict if conditioned
recipe.body: Given information removes impossible values from the sample space.

recipe.title: Measure favorable length
recipe.body: For disjoint favorable intervals add their lengths.

recipe.title: Interpret
recipe.body: The ratio lies between 0 and 1 and represents the eligible fraction.

pitfalls: Uniform waits are not generally memoryless.
For a conditional uniform event, use the remaining eligible length as denominator.

title: Standardize and read a normal probability
description: Convert every endpoint to a z-score, read left-tail probabilities Φ(z), then subtract or complement for the requested event.
recognize: The variable is Normal(μ,σ²).
A probability is requested for above, below, or between numerical thresholds.

recipe.title: Read μ and σ
recipe.body: The second normal parameter is variance. Take its square root if it is supplied as a number.

recipe.title: Standardize every boundary
recipe.body: Subtract the mean and divide by standard deviation.

recipe.title: Read the left-tail table
recipe.body: The supplied table is Φ(z)=P(Z≤z). For negative z, use symmetry.

recipe.title: Match the event
recipe.body: Use the left tail, its complement, or the difference of two left tails.

pitfalls: Divide by standard deviation, not variance.
An upper tail needs 1−Φ(z).
Round z only when necessary for the table.

title: Reverse a normal probability to find a threshold
description: A percentile gives a probability and asks for a value. Find the matching standard normal z, then reverse standardization.
recognize: Only a specified percentage exceeds the unknown threshold.
At least a specified percentage must finish before an unknown time limit.

recipe.title: Convert to a left-tail probability
recipe.body: A right-tail fraction α means the left-tail fraction is 1−α.

recipe.title: Find the matching z
recipe.body: Locate p in the table body; its row and column give z. Interpolation or a supplied z may be used.

recipe.title: Undo standardization
recipe.body: Multiply z by σ and add μ to return to the original units.

recipe.title: Check its position
recipe.body: A percentile above 50% should lie above the mean. If rounding a guaranteed time limit, round upward.

pitfalls: Exceedance percentage is a right tail, not Φ(z).
The threshold has the same units as the original variable.

title: Use exponential waiting-time probabilities
description: Constant-rate Poisson arrivals give exponential waiting times. Match time units, then choose the survival function, CDF, or interval difference.
recognize: Time until the next event at a stable rate is requested.
Exponential(rate λ) is supplied.

recipe.title: Match units
recipe.body: Convert rate or duration so λt is dimensionless.
recipe.formula: λ per minute = λ per hour /60

recipe.title: Choose the event formula
recipe.body: More than is survival; within is a CDF.

recipe.title: For between, subtract tails
recipe.body: The probability surviving a minus surviving b is the interval area.

recipe.title: Connect waiting and counts
recipe.body: No arrival during t is the same event as waiting past t.

pitfalls: Use a rate, not the mean waiting time, as λ.
Do not multiply a rate per hour by minutes without converting.

title: Reset an exponential waiting clock
description: Given that an exponential wait has already lasted s, the probability of surviving another t is unchanged from a fresh wait of length t.
recognize: Given T>s and asking for T>s+t, or at least another t units.
A constant-rate exponential model is stated.

recipe.title: Separate elapsed and additional time
recipe.body: The total threshold is s+t; the new wait is t.

recipe.title: Apply memorylessness
recipe.body: Elapsed time does not alter the additional exponential wait.

recipe.title: Evaluate the new survival probability
recipe.body: Keep the rate and extra duration in matching units.

recipe.title: Check assumptions
recipe.body: Aging or time-varying rates can invalidate memorylessness.

pitfalls: Use the extra time, not the total time, in the final exponent.
Do not apply this rule to uniform or normal variables.

title: Choose a model by support, shape, and assumptions
description: A model is useful only if its assumptions describe the situation. Uniform is flat and bounded, normal is symmetric, exponential is a memoryless nonnegative wait.
recognize: The question asks which distribution or scenario is suitable.
Strong skew, clustering, or aging suggests checking assumptions before computing.

recipe.title: Check support
recipe.body: Ask whether outcomes are counts, real measurements, bounded locations, or nonnegative waiting times.

recipe.title: Check shape
recipe.body: Flat, symmetric, or right-skewed shapes suggest different models.
recipe.formula: Uniform flat; normal bell-shaped; exponential decreasing

recipe.title: Check assumptions
recipe.body: Equal lengths, small additive effects, or constant independent arrival rates must be plausible.
recipe.formula: Model assumptions must match the context

pitfalls: A long right tail alone does not prove an exponential model.
A normal model may assign impossible negative times.

title: Compute a weighted discrete mean
description: Multiply every possible value by its probability and add. Subtract entry costs to turn gross reward into net gain.
recognize: A table of possible values and their probabilities is given.
Expected reward, cost, profit, or long-run average is requested.

recipe.title: Build a valid table
recipe.body: List all values and probabilities; probabilities must sum to 1.

recipe.title: Weight each value
recipe.body: More likely values contribute more to the average.

recipe.title: Add the contributions
recipe.body: Include negative values and any entry cost.

recipe.title: Interpret the mean
recipe.body: The mean is a long-run average, not necessarily a possible or guaranteed outcome.

pitfalls: Do not average the listed values without probability weights.
Gross reward and net gain differ by the entry cost.

title: Compute moments by integrating a density
description: For a continuous variable, use integrals instead of weighted sums. Normalize first, then integrate x f(x) or x² f(x).
recognize: A continuous density is supplied and E[X] or E[X²] is requested.
An expectation is an average weighted by density, not an ordinary integral of x alone.

recipe.title: Normalize the density
recipe.body: If an unknown c is present, find it using total area 1.

recipe.title: Choose the moment
recipe.body: For the first moment use x; for the second moment use x².

recipe.title: Integrate over support
recipe.body: Use the same support as the PDF and evaluate upper minus lower.

recipe.title: Check units and range
recipe.body: E[X] lies within bounded support; E[X²] has squared units.

pitfalls: E[X²] generally differs from (E[X])².
Multiply by the PDF before integrating.

title: Compute variance and standard deviation
description: Find the first and second moments, then subtract the square of the mean. Standard deviation is the square root of variance.
recognize: Spread, risk, variance, or standard deviation is requested.
A mean and second moment are available or can be calculated.

recipe.title: Compute the mean
recipe.body: For discrete values use weighted sums; for continuous values use density integrals.

recipe.title: Compute the second raw moment
recipe.body: Square each possible value before weighting.

recipe.title: Subtract the squared mean
recipe.body: This removes location and leaves spread around the mean.

recipe.title: Take a square root if requested
recipe.body: Variance has squared units; standard deviation has original units.

pitfalls: Never confuse E[X²] with variance.
Variance cannot be negative; a negative result indicates an error.

title: Average a transformed payoff or penalty
description: Evaluate the function at each outcome before averaging, or integrate g(x) against the original density. No new distribution is needed.
recognize: Expected g(X), a squared penalty, or a polynomial compensation is requested.
A nonlinear function of X means substituting only the mean is usually incorrect.

recipe.title: Write the function
recipe.body: Identify exactly what is being paid or measured at each outcome.

recipe.title: Transform before averaging
recipe.body: For a table compute g(x) at every listed x. For a density multiply g(x) by f(x).

recipe.title: Use linearity for polynomials
recipe.body: Separate constant, linear, and quadratic terms into known moments.

recipe.title: Compare carefully
recipe.body: Replacing X by its mean loses the variance contribution in a quadratic.

pitfalls: In general E[g(X)]≠g(E[X]).
A constant can leave expectation; a nonlinear function usually cannot.

title: Transform means and variances
description: Adding a constant shifts the mean but not spread. Multiplying by b scales the mean by b and variance by b².
recognize: Y=a+bX is given, including unit conversions and score transformations.
Mean or variance of X or Y is required.

recipe.title: Identify the shift and scale
recipe.body: Write the transformation as a+bX.

recipe.title: Transform or reverse the mean
recipe.body: Use the first power of b for expectation.

recipe.title: Transform or reverse variance
recipe.body: Use the square of b; the constant a contributes no variance.

recipe.title: If averaging squared distance
recipe.body: Distance from a target c includes spread plus squared bias.

pitfalls: The shift a does not add to variance.
Variance uses b² even if b is negative.

title: Combine random variables and repeated trials
description: Means always add linearly. Variances need dependence information: add covariance terms or use independence to remove them.
recognize: A total or a weighted sum aX+bY is requested.
Repeated independent outcomes or a covariance value is stated.

recipe.title: Combine means
recipe.body: Independence is unnecessary for this step.

recipe.title: Read dependence information
recipe.body: Independence gives covariance 0. Otherwise retain the covariance term.

recipe.title: Square weights for variance
recipe.body: For n independent identically distributed outcomes, multiply variance by n.

recipe.title: Compute the standard deviation last
recipe.body: It is the square root of the total variance.

pitfalls: Do not add standard deviations to obtain the SD of a sum.
Expected counts may be fractional even when actual counts are integers.

title: Count a union with inclusion–exclusion
description: Add single-set counts, subtract pair overlaps, and add triple overlap; subtract the union from the population to count none.
recognize: Three overlapping groups are given, including all pair and triple intersections.
How many use none means the complement of a union.

recipe.title: Define the union
recipe.body: At least one means membership in A∪B∪C.

recipe.title: Correct overlap counts
recipe.body: Add singles, subtract all pair overlaps, then add the triple.

recipe.title: Take the complement
recipe.body: Remove everyone using at least one from the full population.

pitfalls: Pair intersections include people in all three unless stated otherwise.

title: Arrange distinct objects with a consecutive block
description: Treat the designated consecutive objects as one unit, arrange the units, then arrange objects inside that block.
recognize: Certain distinct books must stay together but can be in any internal order.
Order matters, so use factorial arrangements rather than combinations.

recipe.title: Form one block
recipe.body: Collapse k designated items into one super-item.

recipe.title: Arrange all units
recipe.body: The block can occupy any unit position.

recipe.title: Arrange inside the block
recipe.body: The k distinct designated items have k! orders.

pitfalls: A block still needs its internal k! arrangements unless order is fixed.

title: Count conditional samples without replacement
description: For equally likely unordered samples, count favorable eligible samples and divide by all samples satisfying the condition.
recognize: Tokens are sampled without replacement, order is irrelevant, and given information restricts the sample.
Exactly r red tokens requires choosing red and other-color subsets.

recipe.title: Choose combinations
recipe.body: Sampling without replacement with no order uses C(n,r).

recipe.title: Count the conditional denominator
recipe.body: Subtract samples excluded by the given event.

recipe.title: Count the numerator within the condition
recipe.body: For exactly two red and one blue multiply the separate choices.

recipe.title: Divide
recipe.body: All unordered samples are equally likely, so counts give the conditional ratio.

pitfalls: The denominator must respect the given information.
Do not use binomial probabilities for sampling without replacement.

title: Use Bayes after two conditionally independent positives
description: Square positive-test probabilities only within each condition group, then normalize the two possible groups.
recognize: Prevalence, sensitivity, false-positive rate, and two positive results are given.
Tests are independent conditional on true condition status.

recipe.title: Define the groups
recipe.body: D means having the condition; Dᶜ means not having it.

recipe.title: Multiply within each group
recipe.body: Conditional independence allows two positive-test likelihoods to multiply.

recipe.title: Weight by prevalence
recipe.body: Compute joint positive probabilities in both groups.

recipe.title: Normalize with Bayes
recipe.body: Divide the condition-positive joint event by all ways of obtaining two positives.

pitfalls: P(D|++) differs from sensitivity P(++|D).
Conditional independence does not imply unconditional independence of the test results.

title: Condition a geometric first-success time
description: Geometric(p) counts trials through the first success. Use q^k for surviving k trials, and normalize or reset the remaining wait.
recognize: Independent trials with constant success chance continue until the first success.
Given the first success has not occurred yet, geometric memorylessness can reset the trial count.

recipe.title: Set q=1−p
recipe.body: Surviving k attempts means k failures.

recipe.title: Translate endpoints carefully
recipe.body: Including attempt a means X>a−1, while excluding after b means X>b.

recipe.title: Apply the condition
recipe.body: Divide by its probability or reset after known failures.
recipe.formula: P(A|B)=P(A∩B)/P(B); X>s ⇒ X−s is a fresh geometric wait

recipe.title: Check indexing
recipe.body: The first success trial count starts at 1, not 0.

pitfalls: One-off exponent errors are common at inclusive endpoints.

title: Read CDF jumps, transform values, and condition
description: For a discrete variable, the probability of a value is the jump in the CDF. Transform each possible value before selecting the event.
recognize: A stepwise CDF is supplied, followed by Y=g(X) and conditional probability.
Individual points of a discrete distribution can have positive probability.

recipe.title: Recover masses
recipe.body: Subtract the CDF immediately before each value from the CDF at that value.

recipe.title: Apply the transformation
recipe.body: Make a table of x and g(x) to see which x values satisfy the requested Y event.

recipe.title: Restrict to the condition
recipe.body: Only x values allowed by the given event enter the denominator.

pitfalls: Use CDF differences as masses; CDF heights are accumulated probabilities.

title: Use a binomial PMF under a count condition
description: Binomial counts successes in fixed independent trials. Sum the requested counts and divide by the probability of the conditioning event.
recognize: Fixed n independent trials with equal success probability p.
A count probability is requested given X≥k.

recipe.title: Identify n and p
recipe.body: Confirm fixed trials, independent outcomes, and constant p.

recipe.title: Compute the favorable counts
recipe.body: Use the binomial PMF for each requested integer value.

recipe.title: Compute the eligible probability
recipe.body: A lower-tail exclusion often gives a shorter calculation.

recipe.title: Divide
recipe.body: The favorable event must also satisfy the condition.

pitfalls: Normalize after conditioning; an unconditional PMF alone is insufficient.

title: Use Poisson counts over the stated interval
description: Convert the rate and interval into a Poisson mean, compute favorable counts, then normalize for any given count restriction.
recognize: Counts of requests/events at a constant rate over a duration.
A count probability is requested given at least one event.

recipe.title: Scale the mean
recipe.body: Rate times duration gives expected count for this interval.

recipe.title: Use the count PMF
recipe.body: Insert λ and integer count j.

recipe.title: Use complements for tails
recipe.body: At least one excludes only zero; at least three excludes 0,1,2.

recipe.title: Condition if needed
recipe.body: Divide favorable probability by eligible probability.

pitfalls: The hourly rate is not always the λ for the requested interval.

title: Combine independent component failure events
description: Use complements for at least one and add disjoint cases for exactly one. Multiply probabilities within each independent case.
recognize: Independent components have individual failure probabilities.
Exactly one fails given at least one fails is requested.

recipe.title: Find no failures
recipe.body: Independence allows all survival probabilities to multiply.

recipe.title: Take the complement
recipe.body: At least one is every case except none.

recipe.title: Enumerate exactly one
recipe.body: Each case has one failure and all other components surviving. These cases are disjoint.

recipe.title: Condition
recipe.body: Exactly one is a subset of at least one.

pitfalls: Adding failure probabilities counts multiple failures repeatedly.

title: Normalize and sum a finite PMF
description: A discrete PMF has nonnegative masses summing to 1. Find c using a sum, then sum the masses in the event.
recognize: p(x)=c h(x) for integer x in a finite support.
Do not integrate because the variable is discrete.

recipe.title: List support values
recipe.body: Only stated integer values have probability.

recipe.title: Set total mass to 1
recipe.body: Sum h(x) and solve for c.

recipe.title: Sum the requested event
recipe.body: Add its point probabilities, or subtract excluded ones from 1.

pitfalls: Discrete probabilities use sums; densities use integrals.

title: Read standard distribution means and variances
description: When a named distribution is given, the formula sheet supplies its mean and variance. Check the parameter convention and units before substituting.
recognize: A named distribution is given and only mean, variance, or SD is requested.
The exponential parameter is a rate; the geometric variable counts trials through first success.

recipe.title: Identify the parameter convention
recipe.body: Read the distribution name, support, and units. For N(μ,σ²), the second parameter is variance.
recipe.formula: Exp(λ): λ is rate; Geometric(p): X=1,2,…

recipe.title: Choose the matching row
recipe.body: Use the supplied formula sheet rather than integrating or summing from scratch.
recipe.formula: U(a,b): mean=(a+b)/2, variance=(b−a)²/12; Exp(λ): mean=1/λ, variance=1/λ²

recipe.title: Substitute and take a square root if needed
recipe.body: Variance has squared units. SD returns to the original units.

recipe.title: Check discrete formulas
recipe.body: Binomial counts fixed trials; geometric counts trials until first success; Poisson counts events in an interval.
recipe.formula: Bin(n,p): mean=np, variance=np(1−p); Geom(p): mean=1/p, variance=(1−p)/p²; Pois(λ): mean=variance=λ

pitfalls: Exponential mean is 1/rate, not the rate.
Standard deviation is not variance.
Geometric formulas change if the variable counts failures rather than trials.
